★★★★☆  The Map of Small Things – reviewed by Kai, 14
If you like adventure stories with heart, this is for you. Thirteen-year-old Leila finds a hand-drawn map in her late grandfather's coat and follows it across Istanbul.
The best part? The city feels alive – spice markets, ferries, rooftop cats. I could almost smell the simit.
The middle drags a little (too many clues, not enough danger), but the ending made me text my own grandad.
Read it if: you love puzzles, families and food. Skip it if: you need explosions.

Read the following film review on a student film blog.

Tidewater (12A) ★★★★☆
Director Ana Moreno's debut follows two sisters in a Chilean fishing village as the sea swallows their town, house by house.
The cinematography is breathtaking: long, wide shots of grey water make the people look painfully small, while handheld close-ups during the storm put you right in the boat.
The script stumbles in the middle – a romance subplot goes nowhere – but the final ten minutes, almost silent, left our whole row in tears.
Verdict: a quiet film about a loud problem. Bring tissues.

items.markingKey: A strong review supports its opinions with specific evidence from the film (scenes, techniques, performances). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Camera work matters more than dialogue in film."
items.answer: Camera work is central to film's meaning, but it works with dialogue, sound and performance; the strongest scenes combine them.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: film is a visual medium; images show emotion without words. Arguments against: dialogue reveals character and plot; sound and performance matter too. Supported judgement: Camera work is central to film's meaning, but it works with dialogue, sound and performance; the strongest scenes combine them.

items.stem: "Sound is more important than image in creating fear in horror films." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Sound often triggers fear, but it works with mise-en-scène and camera; together they create horror.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: music and silence manipulate emotion; jump scares rely on sound. Arguments against: dark images and framing create dread; sound without image loses meaning. items.stem: "Genre conventions make films predictable." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Conventions can feel predictable, but they also give pleasure and a framework that inventive films build on or subvert.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: audiences can guess what will happen; repetitive formulas. Arguments against: conventions create satisfying expectations; skilful films play with them. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "wide (long) shot"?
options: A shot that shows a whole setting and a figure's place within it
A shot looking down on (high) or up at (low) a subject, making it seem weak or powerful
High-key lighting is bright and even; low-key lighting has strong shadows and darkness
An evaluative article about a film, combining a brief summary, analysis and a verdict
items.answer: A shot that shows a whole setting and a figure's place within it
items.markingKey: A. "wide (long) shot" is a shot that shows a whole setting and a figure's place within it.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "lighting (high-key / low-key)"?
options: High-key lighting is bright and even; low-key lighting has strong shadows and darkness
Sound added for the audience only, such as background music or a voice-over
Sound from one scene that continues into the next, linking them
A category of film with recognisable conventions, such as horror, romance, science fiction or action
items.answer: High-key lighting is bright and even; low-key lighting has strong shadows and darkness
items.markingKey: A. "lighting (high-key / low-key)" is high-key lighting is bright and even; low-key lighting has strong shadows and darkness.

items.stem: Distinguish between following conventions and subverting conventions.
items.answer: Following conventions meets audience expectations (a haunted house in horror); subverting them deliberately breaks expectations (a ghost who is friendly) for surprise or comment.
items.markingKey: Following conventions meets audience expectations (a haunted house in horror); subverting them deliberately breaks expectations (a ghost who is friendly) for surprise or comment. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why using film vocabulary improves a review.
items.answer: Terms like "handheld close-ups" explain precisely how a film creates effects and build the reviewer's credibility.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Terms like "handheld close-ups" explain precisely how a film creates effects and build the reviewer's credibility. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly explain why directors vary shot distance.
items.answer: Different distances control what the audience sees and feels – wide shots establish context, close-ups create intimacy and reveal emotion.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Different distances control what the audience sees and feels – wide shots establish context, close-ups create intimacy and reveal emotion. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between diegetic sound and non-diegetic sound.
items.answer: Diegetic sound comes from within the story world and characters can hear it; non-diegetic sound (soundtrack, voice-over) is added for the audience only.
items.markingKey: Diegetic sound comes from within the story world and characters can hear it; non-diegetic sound (soundtrack, voice-over) is added for the audience only. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Read the following extract from an original film script.

EXT. MUMBAI ROOFTOP – NIGHT
Rain lashes the concrete. Neon signs bleed colour into puddles.
CLOSE-UP: ARJUN (16), soaked, clutching a crumpled acceptance letter.
WIDE SHOT: the city stretches to the horizon; Arjun is tiny at the edge of the roof.
SOUND: traffic below fades. Only rain. Then – his phone buzzes.
INSERT – PHONE SCREEN: "Dad: Come home. We'll talk."
Arjun looks at the letter, then at the city. Slowly, he folds the letter into his pocket.
CUT TO BLACK.

Analyse how camera shots and editing are used in this extract.
items.answer: Camera: the close-up on the letter shows its importance to Arjun; the wide shot makes him tiny against the vast city, showing how small and alone he feels; the insert shot puts the father's message in front of the audience. Sound: the fading traffic leaves only rain, isolating Arjun; the buzz breaks the silence. Editing: the cut to black ends on suspense.
items.markingKey: Camera: the close-up on the letter shows its importance to Arjun; the wide shot makes him tiny against the vast city, showing how small and alone he feels; the insert shot puts the father's message in front of the audience. Sound: the fading traffic leaves only rain, isolating Arjun; the buzz breaks the silence. Editing: the cut to black ends on suspense. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

items.stem:
Read the following description of a horror film trailer.

0:00 – Black screen. A child's music box plays slowly.
0:05 – Bright, sunny shots: a family moves into a farmhouse. Upbeat guitar.
0:15 – The music box again, louder. Quick cuts: a door swinging shut; a shadow on the stairs; the daughter staring at a wall.
0:25 – Silence. Close-up: the daughter turns to camera. "She says we can stay... if we're quiet."
0:28 – A crash of sound. Title: HUSH. In cinemas October.

Analyse the effect of the movement from calm to chaos in the text.
items.answer: The movement from calm to chaos: the trailer sets up normality and then disrupts it, mirroring a horror plot and building to a jump scare.

items.answer: Many films are hybrids (romantic comedy, science-fiction horror), combining conventions of more than one genre.

items.stem:
Read the following film review on a student film blog.

Tidewater (12A) ★★★★☆
Director Ana Moreno's debut follows two sisters in a Chilean fishing village as the sea swallows their town, house by house.
The cinematography is breathtaking: long, wide shots of grey water make the people look painfully small, while handheld close-ups during the storm put you right in the boat.
The script stumbles in the middle – a romance subplot goes nowhere – but the final ten minutes, almost silent, left our whole row in tears.
Verdict: a quiet film about a loud problem. Bring tissues.

Who is the target audience of the text? Refer to two details that suggest this audience.
items.answer: Students and young film fans who read a film blog; the age rating and casual verdict ("Bring tissues") suit them. Supporting evidence: "left our whole row in tears" (personal response) – the reaction of real viewers is evidence of the film's emotional power.
